{{Short description|Process calculus in which names are quoted processes}}

The '''reflective higher-order calculus''', usually abbreviated '''rho calculus''' and often written '''ρ-calculus''' in the literature, is a [[process calculus]] introduced by L. Gregory Meredith and Matthias Radestock in 2005.<ref name="MR2005" /> It is a variant of the [[Pi-calculus|π-calculus]] in which there is no separate, primitive sort of channel names: names are ''quoted processes'', so that the theory of names is generated by, and wholly determined by, the theory of processes.<ref name="MR2005" /><ref name="Lybech2022" />

Because a name can be unquoted — "dropped" — to run the process it encodes, the calculus supports [[Reflective programming|reflection]] in the sense of [[Brian Cantwell Smith]]: a program can turn running code into data, compute with that data, and reinstate it as running code.<ref name="Lybech2022" /> Higher-order process mobility, of the kind added as an extension in [[Higher-order pi calculus|higher-order π-calculus]], appears in the rho calculus as a special case of reflection, namely the case in which the transmitted code is reinstated without modification.<ref name="Lybech2022" /><ref name="Bendixen2022" /> The calculus also dispenses with the name-restriction operator ν: fresh names are produced by quoting, so name generation is accounted for inside the language rather than assumed as an ambient mechanism.<ref name="Lybech2022" />

The rho calculus is the computational model underlying the contract language [[Rholang]] and the blockchain platforms built on it.<ref name="MPC" /> Its relative expressiveness has been studied in the literature on encodability and separation, where it has been shown that the π-calculus can be encoded in the rho calculus but not conversely, under the standard criteria for a valid encoding.<ref name="Lybech2022" /><ref name="Lybech2024" />

{{TOC limit|3}}

== Background and motivation ==

The π-calculus is parametric in its treatment of names: it assumes a countably infinite set of atomic names and provides a theory of processes communicating over them, leaving open what those names actually are. Implementations resolve this externally, for example by interpreting names as TCP/IP ports.<ref name="MR2005" /> A related question concerns the restriction operator (ν''x'')''P'', which declares a name ''x'' whose visibility is limited to ''P'': how a genuinely fresh ''x'' is to be chosen is straightforward for a single machine but less obvious for a distributed system.<ref name="Lybech2022" />

Meredith and Radestock's response was to ask for a ''closed'' theory of processes, in which names are built by a syntax generated from a finite set of elements, rather than assumed.<ref name="MR2005" /><ref name="Lybech2022" /> The choice they made is that a name is a quoted process, written <math>@P</math> (also written <math>\ulcorner P \urcorner</math> in parts of the literature). Since processes in turn contain names, this makes the two syntactic categories mutually recursive.<ref name="Lybech2022" />

== Syntax ==

The grammar defines processes and names simultaneously:

:<math>P, Q ::= \mathbf{0} \;\mid\; P \mid Q \;\mid\; x(y).P \;\mid\; x\langle P \rangle \;\mid\; {*}x</math>
:<math>x, y ::= @P</math>

The constructs are:<ref name="Lybech2022" /><ref name="Bendixen2022" />

* <math>\mathbf{0}</math>, the '''null''' or inactive process;
* <math>P \mid Q</math>, the '''parallel composition''' of ''P'' and ''Q'';
* <math>x(y).P</math>, '''input''': a blocking operation that waits for a name on the channel ''x'' and binds the received name to ''y'' in the continuation ''P'';
* <math>x\langle P \rangle</math>, '''lift''' (output): quotes the process ''P'', thereby creating the name <math>@P</math>, and sends it on ''x'';
* <math>{*}x</math>, '''drop''': removes the quotes from the name ''x'' and runs the process inside;
* <math>@P</math>, '''quote''': the name that codes the process ''P''.

Input is the only binder. There is no restriction operator and no replication operator; both are definable (see [[#Expressiveness|Expressiveness]] below).<ref name="Lybech2022" />

The concrete syntax of Rholang renders input as <code>for (y <- x) { P }</code>, output as <code>x!(P)</code>, drop as <code>*x</code> and quote as <code>@P</code>; this notation is also used in some of the theoretical literature.<ref name="StayMeredith2017" />

== Equational theory ==

Because names carry structure, the equational theory of the calculus involves two mutually recursive relations: [[structural congruence]] <math>\equiv</math> on processes and ''name equivalence'' <math>\equiv_{\mathcal{N}}</math> on names.<ref name="Lybech2022" />

=== Name equivalence ===

Name equivalence is the least equivalence on names closed under the rules

:<math>\frac{P \equiv Q}{@P \equiv_{\mathcal{N}} @Q} \qquad \frac{x \equiv_{\mathcal{N}} y}{@{*}x \equiv_{\mathcal{N}} y}</math>

The first says that quoting structurally congruent processes yields the same name; the second lets nested layers of quoting and dropping cancel.<ref name="Lybech2022" />

=== Structural congruence ===

Structural congruence is the least congruence on processes containing [[Lambda calculus#Alpha equivalence|α-equivalence]] and the [[commutative monoid]] laws for parallel composition with <math>\mathbf{0}</math> as unit. The congruence rules take an unusual form, since names must themselves be compared: for instance, concluding <math>x_1(y_1).P_1 \equiv x_2(y_2).P_2</math> requires <math>x_1 \equiv_{\mathcal{N}} x_2</math> together with agreement of the continuations after renaming the bound names apart.<ref name="Lybech2022" />

This creates a mutual recursion between structural congruence, α-equivalence and name equivalence. Meredith and Radestock showed that the recursion is well founded and terminates, because the sets of processes and names are themselves well founded, with least elements <math>\mathbf{0}</math> and <math>@\mathbf{0}</math>.<ref name="MR2005" /><ref name="Bendixen2022" />

=== Substitution ===

Substitution <math>P\{x/y\}</math> replaces not only ''y'' but every name equivalent to ''y''. It does not descend into processes underneath a quote: a quoted process is data, and is left untouched unless the whole name is itself the target of the substitution.<ref name="Lybech2022" /><ref name="Bendixen2022" />

The substitution used in the reduction semantics additionally accounts for drop, replacing <math>{*}x</math> by the process ''P'' when <math>x</math> is name equivalent to <math>@P</math>. This is the only mechanism by which a drop is ever executed, with the consequence that dropping a free name is a deadlock, since no runtime substitution can reach it.<ref name="Lybech2022" />

== Reduction ==

The operational semantics is given as a [[reduction system]] with the rules for parallel composition and structural congruence familiar from the π-calculus, together with a single communication rule:<ref name="Lybech2022" />

:<math>[\rho\text{-}\mathrm{COM}] \quad \frac{x_1 \equiv_{\mathcal{N}} x_2}{x_1(y).P \;\mid\; x_2\langle Q \rangle \;\longrightarrow\; P\{@Q/y\}}</math>

:<math>[\rho\text{-}\mathrm{PAR}] \quad \frac{P_1 \longrightarrow P_1'}{P_1 \mid P_2 \longrightarrow P_1' \mid P_2} \qquad [\rho\text{-}\mathrm{STRUCT}] \quad \frac{P_1 \equiv P_1' \quad P_1' \longrightarrow P_2' \quad P_2' \equiv P_2}{P_1 \longrightarrow P_2}</math>

The communication rule differs from its π-calculus counterpart in that the two subjects need only be ''name equivalent'', rather than syntactically identical; in calculi with atomic names, exact equality is usually required implicitly.<ref name="Lybech2022" /> Deciding whether a communication can fire therefore involves a computation on names, and the relationship between name equality in substitution and name equality in synchronisation is one of the questions the calculus was designed to raise.<ref name="MR2005" />

=== Example ===

Sending a process and immediately running it on receipt:

:<math>x(y).{*}y \;\mid\; x\langle Q \rangle \;\longrightarrow\; {*}@Q \;\equiv\; Q</math>

The output quotes ''Q'' into a name, the input binds that name to ''y'', and the drop in the continuation unquotes it, so that ''Q'' begins executing in the receiver's context.

== Reflection, names and namespaces ==

Since <math>{*}@P \equiv P</math>, quoting and dropping are mutually inverse, and code and data are two views of the same term. Three consequences distinguish the calculus from the π-calculus.

'''Names are generated by the program.''' Fresh names are made by quoting, so freshness is a property the program must establish rather than a service the calculus provides.<ref name="Lybech2022" /> Standard "static quoting" techniques generate countably many distinct names from any starting name — for example by repeatedly forming <math>@(x\langle \mathbf{0}\rangle)</math> — which shows that a countably infinite supply of π-calculus names can be implemented inside the calculus.<ref name="Lybech2022" />

'''New names appearing at runtime are free.''' Because there is no ν operator to bind them, names created during reduction are free in the continuation and hence observable. This is exactly the feature exploited in the separation result described below.<ref name="Lybech2022" />

'''Names stratify.''' The ''quote depth'' of a name — roughly, how many layers of quoting it carries — is preserved by name equivalence, so names of different quote depth can never be equivalent. Collections of names may then be organised into ''namespaces'' generated by name contexts, and namespaces rooted at inequivalent names are disjoint.<ref name="Lybech2022" /> Namespaces play the role that scoping plays elsewhere, and have been used to supply both freshness and polarisation at the level of types.<ref name="PolicyAsTypes" />

== Behavioural theory ==

Since the calculus has no ν operator, the usual barbed equivalences require adjustment before they can be compared with those of calculi that do. Meredith and Radestock defined an observation predicate parametrised by a set <math>\mathcal{N}</math> of names, so that only names in that set may be observed; barbs are then taken up to name equivalence.<ref name="MR2005" /><ref name="Lybech2022" /> The associated notions of <math>\mathcal{N}</math>-restricted barbed bisimulation and its weak counterpart specialise to ordinary barbed bisimilarity when <math>\mathcal{N}</math> is the set of all names.<ref name="Lybech2022" />

== Expressiveness ==

=== Encoding the π-calculus ===

Meredith and Radestock gave an encoding of the asynchronous, choice-free π-calculus into the rho calculus, together with an account of ν and of replication, and claimed full abstraction with respect to weak barbed bisimilarity.<ref name="MR2005" /> Replication is obtained from higher-order mobility by a construction analogous to the [[Lambda calculus#Undecidability of equivalence|Ω combinator]]: a process that runs what it receives while making a copy of it available again will, when sent a copy of itself, reproduce indefinitely.<ref name="Lybech2022" />

In 2022 Stian Lybech showed that this encoding is incorrect, identifying two errors, both arising from an unstated invariant on the name parameters carried by the translation.<ref name="Lybech2022" /> Lybech then gave a different encoding and proved it correct against criteria close to those of [[Daniele Gorla|Gorla]], adapted to accommodate parametrised translations by adding a requirement of parameter independence. The new encoding isolates runtime name generation in a single contextual "name server" process that hands out consecutive names from one namespace.<ref name="Lybech2022" /><ref name="Lybech2024" />

=== Separation from the π-calculus ===

Lybech also proved a separation result: there is no encoding of the rho calculus into the π-calculus satisfying the same criteria, for any behavioural equivalence preserving reduction, observability and substitution.<ref name="Lybech2022" /> The argument turns on the ability of the rho calculus to create new ''free'' names during reduction, which are therefore both observable and substitutable — a step that cannot be matched in a calculus whose names are atomic and cannot be composed at runtime.<ref name="Lybech2022" />

Since [[Davide Sangiorgi|Sangiorgi]]'s encoding of higher-order π-calculus into the π-calculus satisfies the criteria, it follows that the rho calculus cannot be encoded in higher-order π-calculus either. The feature that resists encoding is thus reflection rather than higher-order communication as such.<ref name="Lybech2022" />

== Variations ==

=== Variations of the communication rule ===

The single communication rule is a natural site for variation, since it fixes both when two names count as the same and what survives an interaction.

; Annihilation
: In the standard rule the output is consumed and the input's continuation proceeds under a substitution. An alternative, discussed in the RChain lecture series on the design of computational calculi, treats a matched input and output as ''annihilating'' one another, with the choice of annihilation regime determining the set theory that the reflective structure gives rise to.<ref name="DoCC2" /><ref name="DoCC41" />{{better source needed|date=July 2026}}
: <!-- TODO (Meredith): a peer-reviewed or otherwise citable statement of the annihilation rule is needed here, ideally with the rule itself. Wikipedia will not accept a reconstruction from an unpublished note. -->

; Contextualised communication
: A further variant makes the firing of a communication depend on the surrounding context rather than on the redex alone.<ref name="DoCC41" />{{better source needed|date=July 2026}}

; Approximate ("fuzzy") name matching
: <!-- TODO (Meredith): this subsection is deliberately left empty pending a source. As written, the natural reading is that the premise x1 ≡_N x2 of the comm rule is weakened from an equivalence to a graded or approximate relation, with a degree of match attached to the reduction. I have not written that up, because I could not find it in the published literature and I do not want to put an unsourced reconstruction into a draft that a reviewer will read. Supply the reference and I will write the subsection. -->

; Polyadic and joined input
: Practical descendants of the calculus generalise input to receive several names at once and to join several receipts into a single synchronisation, and add a persistent form of input that is not consumed when it fires.<ref name="MPC" />

=== Structural variations ===

; Mixed summation
: The calculus as presented has no choice operator. Adding a guarded [[Summation (process algebra)|summation]] in which input and output guards may appear in the same sum — ''mixed'' choice — is a well-studied dividing line in the theory of process calculi, since mixed choice is not encodable into its absence under standard criteria.<ref name="PetersYoshida" />
: <!-- TODO (Meredith): as above, a citable presentation of the mixed-summation rho calculus is needed. The general mixed-choice literature is cited here only as context; it says nothing about the rho calculus specifically, and on its own will not carry the subsection. -->

; Localised rho calculus
: The localised rho calculus adds ''locations'': named, bounded regions of computation arranged in a hierarchy, which processes may enter and leave. Migration between locations is then a form of higher-order communication. The calculus was given a sound system of binary [[session type]]s.<ref name="Tran2019" />

; Primitive name restriction
: Implementations and several later presentations reintroduce a primitive <code>new</code> operator for name restriction as a convenience, rather than relying on quoting to generate fresh names.<ref name="MPC" />

== Namespace logic ==

Namespace logic is a [[Hennessy–Milner logic]] for the rho calculus, introduced by Meredith and Radestock in 2005.<ref name="NamespaceLogic" /> As in other spatial and modal logics for concurrency, formulae denote sets of processes; what is distinctive is that, because names are quoted processes, a further class of formulae emerges that denotes ''sets of names''.<ref name="NamespaceLogic" />

This gives a logical handle on collections of channels. Meredith and Radestock illustrated two applications: formulae constraining the ranges of names on which a process may respond, comparable to a static port-access constraint in a firewall configuration; and, reading names as data, formulae corresponding to validation for a fragment of [[XML Schema]].<ref name="NamespaceLogic" />

The idea that name collections can be specified logically also underlies the use of namespaces as types, where a type discipline over namespaces supplies both freshness and the polarisation of names used in [[object-capability model|object-capability]] discipline.<ref name="PolicyAsTypes" />

== Type systems ==

The rho calculus can be instantiated as a higher-order [[Psi-calculi|Ψ-calculus]], and a generic type system for higher-order Ψ-calculi therefore yields a type system for it. This is of interest precisely because the separation result blocks the usual route of adapting a first-order type system through an encoding into the π-calculus.<ref name="Bendixen2022" /><ref name="Huttel2024" />

Binary session types have been given for the localised variant,<ref name="Tran2019" /> and namespace-based type disciplines have been proposed for capability-safe programming.<ref name="PolicyAsTypes" />

== Categorical semantics ==

The operational semantics of the rho calculus has been presented using [[Lawvere theory|enriched Lawvere theories]], in which terms are morphisms and rewrites are captured by graph structure, with the quoting and dropping operators replacing replication and restriction.<ref name="StayMeredith2017" /> Related work models the rewrite rules of the π-calculus and its reflective variant as 2-morphisms in a higher category,<ref name="HigherCat" /> and gives a combinator basis, in the style of [[SKI combinator calculus]], for a name-free presentation of the calculus.<ref name="NameFree" />

== Implementations ==

[[Rholang]] is a concurrent programming language obtained by extending the rho calculus with data types, patterns and other conveniences — an "injection" of names that are not merely quoted processes — while retaining its reduction semantics.<ref name="DoCC41" /><ref name="MPC" /> Rholang was developed as the contract language of the RChain blockchain platform, whose execution model is derived directly from the calculus and whose runtime pairs the reduction relation with a [[tuple space]].<ref name="MPC" /><ref name="DoCC41" />

The RChain node implementation, written in [[Scala (programming language)|Scala]], has been continued as the <code>f1r3node</code> project by F1R3FLY.io, which has reimplemented the node and Rholang interpreter in [[Rust (programming language)|Rust]] with the stated aim of higher throughput.<ref name="f1r3node" />{{primary source inline|date=July 2026}} Forks of the codebase are used in the ASI Alliance's chain node.<ref name="asichain" />{{primary source inline|date=July 2026}}
